The Reynolds number range covered in the experiments is 10,000 to 172,000, based on inlet velocity and axial chord.
The freestream turbulence intensity ranges from 0.08% to 4% in the experiments.
The intermittency transport model reproduces the streamwise intermittency distribution of Dhawan and Narasimha and also produces a realistic variation of intermittency in the cross-stream direction.
For the Re=86,000, FSTI=1% case, the computations underpredict the extent of the separation bubble compared to the experiments.
For the Re=172,000 case, the computations underpredict the total pressure loss coefficient compared to the experiments for both FSTI=1% and FSTI=4%.
The onset of separation location moves upstream with decreasing freestream turbulence intensity, and the separated flow region becomes smaller with increasing Reynolds number.
At Re=100,000, the flow separates at x/Cx=0.725 and transitions and reattaches around x/Cx=0.80 in the computations.
At Re=50,000, the separation bubble extends until x/Cx~0.93 in the computations, compared to x/Cx~0.975 in the experiments.
The intermittency model is able to accurately predict the velocity profiles in the separated and transitional regions for the different flow conditions.
The computations show that the cascade losses decrease as the Reynolds number increases from 25,000 to 50,000, due to the reduction in the size of the separated flow region.
